title: Terraform basics
bridge: Terraform is like package.json plus a lockfile, for machines: you write what should exist, and the tool works out the steps. Except it also keeps state, a record of what really exists, and apply changes real infrastructure. It can destroy things, so a person reads every plan.
intro: Every AWS piece from p3 is written down as code in the infrastructure repo. This lesson teaches the loop behind it: write HCL, run plan, read it, apply. We use OpenTofu, the fork our repo runs. Our resource is a local file, so nothing touches the cloud.

picture.caption: Plan compares what you wrote with what state says exists and what is really there; a person reads it and applies.

steps.text: reads what it created last time
refresh: asks the provider what is really there now
prints the difference as a list of actions
a person reads every line, the destroys first
tofu apply makes the changes and updates state

p: Terraform describes infrastructure in HCL, a config language of blocks and name = value lines. Our infrastructure repo runs OpenTofu 1.12.6, the open-source fork of Terraform. The language is the same and the command is tofu.

A provider is a plugin that talks to one API: aws, helm, vault. A resource is one thing the provider manages. The local provider manages files on your disk, which makes it perfect for learning: you can see and delete what it makes.
sections.because: We start with a file because you can watch it appear and disappear, and nothing costs money.

notes.text: Which provider, from where, at which exact version. Our repo pins versions in common.hcl the same way.
resource "<type>" "<name>". Its address is local_file.hello.
${...} puts a value inside a string. path.module is this folder.
The arguments describe the thing. Change one and the plan says what that does.

p: tofu init downloads the providers and writes .terraform.lock.hcl, the lockfile with their checksums. You commit the lockfile, like package-lock.json.

tofu plan compares the config with state and with reality, then prints what it would do. tofu apply prints the same plan, asks for 'yes', and does it. In this lab we pass -auto-approve; in our repo a person types yes after reading.
Two more commands only read your files. tofu fmt fixes the layout of .tf files; with -check it only reports bad files. tofu validate checks names and types, with no state and no cloud.
sections.because: We run plan before apply every time because the plan is the only moment you can stop a mistake.

code.text:
tofu init
tofu plan
tofu apply -auto-approve      # lab only: in the repo a person reads and types yes
cat out/hello.txt

notes.text: Downloads hashicorp/local and writes the lockfile. Run it again after adding a provider or a module.
Reads only. Nothing is created.
Creates the file and writes terraform.tfstate.

sections.h: State: the record of what exists
p: After apply, OpenTofu writes terraform.tfstate, a JSON file that maps each resource address to the real thing it created. Without it, OpenTofu could not tell 'create' from 'already there'.
Delete the file by hand and plan again. State still lists it, the refresh finds it gone, so the plan creates it again. This is drift: reality moved away from state.
State can hold secrets in plain text, so it never goes in git. Our repo keeps it in the S3 bucket rhinohealth-terraform-state, with a lock file so two people cannot apply at once (p4-2).
sections.because: We break the file on purpose because seeing drift once explains most surprising plans.

code.text:
tofu state list
tofu state show local_file.hello | head -4
rm out/hello.txt
tofu plan

notes.text: Every address OpenTofu manages here.
What state recorded about one resource.
Change reality behind OpenTofu's back.
The refresh notices, and the plan puts it back.

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.

p: A variable is an input, like a function parameter. for_each makes one resource per entry of a map; inside, each.key and each.value are the entry. An output is a value the config returns, like a function's return value.
This is the shape of G3-11: one launch template per size. Here each 'template' is a file, so you can see one appear per key.
sections.because: We use for_each over a map because every size gets the same rules, and a new size should be one line.

notes.text: The type is checked: a map of strings. A wrong input fails before any plan.
One resource per key. Their addresses are local_file.launch_template["lite"] and ["full"].
each.key is lite or full; each.value is the instance type.
A for expression, like .map(): the filename of every file.

p: Each resource in a plan has a symbol: + create, ~ update in place, -/+ destroy then create a replacement, - destroy. Inside, an argument marked '# forces replacement' is the reason a resource will be replaced.
For a file, a replacement is harmless. For a VM, a database or a VPC, -/+ means the old one and its data are gone. The summary line counts the actions; read the destroys first.
sections.because: We read the plan symbol by symbol because one -/+ on the wrong resource can delete a database.

code.file: tofu plan after changing full to "m7i.2xlarge" (output trimmed)
code.text:
OpenTofu will perform the following actions:

  # local_file.launch_template["full"] must be replaced
-/+ resource "local_file" "launch_template" {
      ~ content              = <<-EOT # forces replacement
          - instance_type = m8i.2xlarge
          + instance_type = m7i.2xlarge
        EOT
      ~ id                   = "b6bf1b60ea3f15ae2f08f0332d7d3bbc6be5c7a1" -> (known after apply)
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy.

notes.text: The address and the verdict, in words.
-/+ : destroy, then create. The most important symbol to notice.
The reason: this argument cannot change in place.
One replacement counts as 1 to add and 1 to destroy.

callout.text: Agents never run apply or destroy, anywhere. They may write HCL, run fmt, validate and plan, and post a plan a person produced. The missing credentials enforce it (p4-6).

p: A module is a folder of .tf files with variables and outputs. You call it with a module block, like calling a component with props. Every folder you run is itself the root module.

Our repo calls its own modules (modules/aws-vpc-private) and registry modules with a pinned version (terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws 6.5.1 inside it). Resources in a module get the prefix module.<name>. in their address.
sections.because: We wrap resources in modules because the same VPC or pool shape is used in more than one place.

notes.text: A local path: the folder with the module's .tf files. Run tofu init after adding it.
Inputs are the module's variables. Here we pass ours through.
A module's outputs are read as module.<name>.<output>.
A registry module: a source name plus an exact version, like an npm package.

lab.faded: Move the resource into a module. Create modules/pool/main.tf with the variable sizes, the resource (use path.root instead of path.module in filename) and an output files. Replace the resource and output in main.tf with the third version (section 6). Run tofu init, because modules need it too. Left to you: before you run tofu plan, write down the new addresses (hint: they start with module.pool.), then check.
lab.alone: Write ~/academy/tf2/main.tf that makes one file per AZ for the list ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]. Each file holds that AZ's subnet: cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, index). Build the for_each map with a for expression: { for i, az in var.azs : az => i }. Apply, then remove us-east-1b from the list and read what the plan wants to destroy.
lab.done: You can apply and destroy the files and explain why a deleted file comes back. In a replacement plan you can point at the -/+ line and its reason.

quiz.q: You deleted out/hello.txt by hand. What does tofu plan show?

options.text: Nothing to do, because state still lists the file
options.why: Plan refreshes against reality first, so it notices the file is gone.

options.text: local_file.hello will be created: state says it should exist and the refresh finds it missing
An error that state is corrupt

quiz.q: A plan shows -/+ and '# forces replacement' on a VM. What will apply do?

options.why: In place is ~. -/+ is destroy and create.

options.text: Destroy the VM, with its disk, and create a new one
options.why: Read the reason line and decide if that is what you want.
Apply changes real resources; state follows.

quiz.q: Why is .terraform.lock.hcl committed, but terraform.tfstate never is?

options.text: The lockfile pins provider versions for everyone; state records real resources, may hold secrets, and lives in a locked remote backend
options.why: Same idea as committing package-lock.json, but never a database dump.

options.text: Both are generated, so neither is committed
options.why: The lockfile is generated and still committed, like package-lock.json.

options.text: State files are too large for git
options.why: Size is not the problem; secrets and two people applying at once are.

words.plain: The open-source fork of Terraform that our infrastructure repo runs; same HCL, command tofu.
A plugin that talks to one API (aws, helm, vault, local) and manages its resources.
One managed thing, declared as resource "<type>" "<name>" with arguments.
The record of what OpenTofu created, mapping addresses to real things; never in git.
The list of actions OpenTofu would take: + create, ~ update, -/+ replace, - destroy.
Carry out a plan and update state; a person's job, never an agent's.
A folder of .tf files with variables and outputs, called with a module block.

tickets.why: A module that wraps the registry VPC module at a pinned version, with variables and outputs.
Launch templates made with for_each over a sizes map: one resource per key.
CI runs tofu fmt and tofu validate on every module, with no state and no cloud keys.

remember: Write what should exist, read the plan line by line, and let a person apply. State is the record that makes the plan possible.
